A variator (20) and a forward clutch (Fwd/C), arranged in series, are provided between an engine (1) having a starter motor (15) and a driving wheel (7). Sailing stop control is performed in which, upon satisfaction of a sailing entry condition, power transmission is interrupted by the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C), the engine (1) is stopped, and coast travel is carried out.

When the sailing entry condition is satisfied, coast travel is initiated with the rotation stop timing of the variator (20) delayed relative to the rotation stop timing of the engine (1). If an accelerator pedal depression operation occurs after the start of coast travel, the engine (1) is restarted by the starter motor (15). When it is determined that the input and output rotation speeds of the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) have reached a synchronous rotation speed after restart of the engine (1), the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) is reengaged.

Accordingly, shift response from coast travel to normal travel is improved in a change-of-mind situation in which a sailing exit condition is satisfied during the automatic stopping process of the engine.
outputs.L2: A variator (20) and a forward clutch (Fwd/C), arranged one after the other, are installed between an engine (1) equipped with a starter motor (15) and a drive wheel (7). Sailing stop control is carried out when a sailing entry condition is met: the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) cuts off power transmission, the engine (1) is stopped, and the vehicle coasts. Once the sailing entry condition has been satisfied, coasting begins while the stopping of rotation of the variator (20) is made later than the stopping of rotation of the engine (1). If the accelerator pedal is pressed after coasting has started, the starter motor (15) restarts the engine (1). After the engine (1) has restarted, when it is determined that the input and output rotational speeds of the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) have reached a synchronized rotational speed, the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) is engaged again. outputs.L3:
A vehicle drive system includes a variator and a forward clutch arranged in series in a power transmission path between an engine and a driving wheel. The engine is equipped with a starter motor, which is capable of restarting the engine when required. The variator changes the transmission ratio between the engine side and the driving wheel side, while the forward clutch selectively connects and disconnects the power transmission path.

The vehicle is configured to perform sailing stop control. In this control, when predetermined sailing entry conditions are satisfied, power transmission between the engine and the driving wheel is interrupted by disengaging the forward clutch. The engine is then stopped, allowing the vehicle to coast or travel by inertia without engine driving force. This reduces fuel consumption during periods when engine power is not required.

When the vehicle enters the sailing state, the timing at which rotation of the variator stops is delayed relative to the timing at which rotation of the engine stops. In other words, the engine is stopped first, while the variator is allowed to continue rotating for a period of time after engine rotation has ceased. This control helps maintain a favorable rotational state in the transmission during the transition into coast-travel.

If the driver depresses the accelerator pedal while the vehicle is coasting in the sailing state, a request to resume normal driving is detected. In response, the starter motor restarts the engine. After the engine has restarted, the forward clutch is reengaged. The reengagement is performed when the input-side and output-side rotational speeds of the forward clutch have become synchronized, or sufficiently close to synchronization.

By engaging the forward clutch after synchronization of its input and output speeds, clutch engagement shock can be reduced while allowing driving force to be transmitted smoothly. As a result, when the vehicle returns from coast-travel to normal powered driving, response is improved and a smooth transition is achieved.
outputs.L4:
A vehicle sailing stop control system is provided for a vehicle equipped with an engine, a continuously variable transmission including a variator, and a forward clutch arranged in a power transmission path between the engine and driving wheels. The system performs a sailing stop control during vehicle travel when predetermined conditions are satisfied, such as when the driver releases the accelerator pedal and the vehicle is coasting. In this control, the system interrupts the transmission of driving force by disengaging the forward clutch and automatically stops the engine, thereby allowing the vehicle to coast while reducing fuel consumption.

When the sailing stop control is executed, rotation of the engine decreases and eventually stops. At this time, the control system prevents the variator from stopping immediately together with the engine. Instead, the system delays stoppage of rotation of the variator relative to stoppage of engine rotation. By maintaining rotation of the variator for a period after the engine has stopped, the system keeps the transmission in a state that is more favorable for rapid reengagement and torque transmission if the driver subsequently requests acceleration.

If, during this coast-travel state or during the automatic engine stop process, the driver changes their mind and depresses the accelerator pedal, the system cancels the sailing stop control and initiates engine restart. The engine is restarted while the forward clutch remains disengaged, so that the engine can be brought back up to speed without immediately transmitting torque to the drive wheels. During this restart operation, the control system monitors the rotational speed on the input side of the forward clutch and the rotational speed on the output side of the forward clutch.

After the engine has restarted, the system controls the forward clutch so that it is reengaged when the input-side rotational speed and the output-side rotational speed of the clutch are substantially synchronized. Because the variator has been kept rotating for longer than the engine, the speed difference across the forward clutch can be reduced more quickly. As a result, the clutch can be engaged at an earlier and more appropriate timing, while suppressing engagement shock and maintaining drivability.

This control improves response when the driver requests acceleration after an automatic engine stop has begun or while the vehicle is coasting with the engine stopped. In particular, it shortens the delay between accelerator operation and restoration of driving force, while also avoiding abrupt torque transmission caused by engaging the clutch before synchronization. Accordingly, the system achieves both fuel economy improvement through sailing stop control and smooth, responsive vehicle acceleration when the driver changes from a coasting intention to an acceleration intention.

A variator, FWD, and sailing mode are three terms often associated with modern vehicle technology, especially in cars designed for comfort and efficiency.

A **variator** is a key component in a continuously variable transmission, commonly known as a CVT. Instead of using fixed gears like a traditional automatic or manual gearbox, a variator allows the transmission ratio to change smoothly and continuously. This helps the engine operate in its most efficient speed range, improving fuel economy and providing smooth acceleration without noticeable gear shifts.

**FWD**, or front-wheel drive, means that the engine sends power to the front wheels of the vehicle. This layout is popular in many passenger cars because it is compact, efficient, and provides good traction in everyday driving conditions. Since the weight of the engine is usually over the front wheels, FWD vehicles often perform well on wet or slippery roads.

**Sailing** refers to a fuel-saving driving function used in some modern cars. When the driver lifts off the accelerator, the system can disconnect the engine from the drivetrain or reduce engine braking, allowing the vehicle to coast freely. This helps the car maintain momentum with less fuel consumption, especially on flat roads or gentle downhill sections.

Together, a variator, FWD system, and sailing function can contribute to a smoother and more economical driving experience. The variator provides seamless power delivery, FWD offers practical and efficient traction, and sailing helps reduce unnecessary fuel use during coasting. These technologies are especially valuable in urban driving and long-distance travel, where comfort and efficiency are important.

counterfactuals.output:
A vehicle sailing stop control system is provided for a power transmission path in which a variator and a forward clutch are arranged between an engine and drive wheels. During a sailing stop condition, in which the vehicle travels by inertia with the engine stopped, the system releases or reduces engagement of the forward clutch and controls the variator so that stoppage of the variator is delayed relative to engine stoppage. When a request to cancel the sailing stop is detected, the engine is restarted and the variator is controlled to resume rotation while the forward clutch is brought toward engagement.

The control system performs synchronization control of the forward clutch based on the rotational state of the engine side and the drive-wheel side of the transmission. Engagement pressure of the forward clutch is adjusted so that clutch input and output speeds are synchronized before or during re-engagement, thereby suppressing shock and preventing excessive slip. Because the variator is not immediately stopped during sailing stop, or is placed in a condition allowing rapid return to operation, hydraulic pressure and rotational readiness can be secured more quickly at engine restart.

Accordingly, when driving force is again required after sailing, the variator can promptly establish an appropriate speed ratio and the forward clutch can be synchronized and engaged with reduced delay. This improves shift response and acceleration response after engine restart, while maintaining smoothness of clutch engagement and enhancing fuel efficiency through effective sailing stop operation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Convert this technical invention into Japanese-patent-style English: a vehicle coast-travel control with engine (1), starter motor (15), variator (20), Fwd/C, sailing entering condition, sailing quitting condition, restart on accelerator depression, and clutch reengagement at synchronized speeds.
counterfactuals.output:
A coast-travel control apparatus for a vehicle is provided, the vehicle including an engine (1), a starter motor (15) configured to crank the engine (1), a variator (20) provided in a power transmission path between the engine (1) and driving wheels, and a forward clutch (Fwd/C) provided in the power transmission path.

The coast-travel control apparatus comprises a controller configured to determine whether a sailing entering condition is satisfied during travel of the vehicle. When the sailing entering condition is satisfied, the controller stops fuel supply to the engine (1) and releases the forward clutch (Fwd/C), thereby executing sailing travel in which the vehicle travels by inertia with the engine (1) stopped and the power transmission path interrupted.

The controller is further configured to determine whether a sailing quitting condition is satisfied during the sailing travel. When the sailing quitting condition is satisfied, the controller controls the starter motor (15) to restart the engine (1). In a case where the sailing quitting condition is satisfied due to depression of an accelerator pedal by a driver, the controller restarts the engine (1) in response to the accelerator pedal depression.

After the engine (1) has been restarted, the controller controls the variator (20) so as to bring a rotational speed on an engine side of the forward clutch (Fwd/C) and a rotational speed on a driving-wheel side of the forward clutch (Fwd/C) into a synchronized state. When the rotational speeds of the forward clutch (Fwd/C) are synchronized, the controller reengages the forward clutch (Fwd/C), thereby restoring transmission of driving force from the engine (1) to the driving wheels.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the operation and advantage of a transmission control device that performs sailing stop control by interrupting power through a forward clutch, stopping the engine, delaying variator rotation stop, restarting on accelerator operation, and reengaging the clutch when input/output speeds synchronize.
counterfactuals.output:
The transmission control device performs a “sailing stop” control during vehicle coasting to improve fuel economy while maintaining smooth restart performance.

During sailing stop, when predetermined conditions are satisfied, such as the accelerator being released and the vehicle traveling in a suitable speed range, the controller disengages or releases a forward clutch provided in the power transmission path between the engine and the drive wheels. By interrupting the power transmission through the forward clutch, the engine is disconnected from the transmission and drive wheels. The controller then stops the engine, allowing the vehicle to coast by inertia without engine fuel consumption.

At this time, the variator, such as a belt-type continuously variable transmission mechanism, is not stopped immediately. Because the forward clutch is released, rotation from the drive wheels can continue to rotate at least part of the transmission. The controller delays stopping rotation of the variator or maintains variator rotation for a period, so that the transmission remains in a state capable of quickly resuming torque transmission.

When the driver operates the accelerator pedal, indicating a request for driving force, the controller restarts the engine. After restart, the controller monitors the rotational speed on the input side and the rotational speed on the output side of the forward clutch. The forward clutch is reengaged when these speeds are synchronized, or when the speed difference has become sufficiently small.

The advantage of this control is that fuel consumption is reduced because the engine is stopped during coasting, while restart shock is suppressed because the forward clutch is not reengaged until the clutch input and output speeds are matched. Also, by delaying the stop of the variator, the transmission can return to a drive-ready state more quickly, improving acceleration response when the driver depresses the accelerator after sailing stop. Thus, the device achieves both improved fuel economy and smooth, responsive reacceleration.
